COMPANY

Built for the business behind healthcare.

We bring revenue cycle management, data intelligence, credentialing, practice operations, and healthcare technology into one accountable operating model. We connect financial insight to the people and processes needed to act on it; clinical authority remains with your practice.

HOW WE OPERATE

Revenue intelligence with execution behind it.

We built ROOT around a recurring operating problem: denials, aging balances, credentialing delays, and fragmented reports are often managed separately. We connect the financial picture to the work needed to improve it.

We join revenue operations with data intelligence. DIRT is our embedded capability for examining financial signals, explaining exposure, and prioritizing action. We define the operating ownership needed to follow through.

OUR MISSION
Turn revenue intelligence into accountable improvement.

We help US independent physician practices and specialty groups understand revenue constraints, choose practical interventions, and measure progress. We combine people, processes, and technology around agreed business outcomes.

Our vision

We aim to make reliable revenue intelligence and accountable operating support accessible to independent healthcare organizations. We want practice leaders to see what needs attention, understand why it matters, and have a practical path to act.

Who we build for

We focus on US independent physician practices and growing medical groups. Our initial commercial focus includes cardiology, vascular, and multispecialty practices; we also scope other specialty groups and ambulatory surgery centers according to their systems, payer mix, and operating needs.

We use technology to accelerate the work. We keep people accountable for judgment. We support claims with evidence and measure progress against an agreed baseline.

Evidence before assertions

We reconcile source reports, document assumptions, and distinguish findings from estimates. We label demonstrations and never present modeled results as client outcomes.

Automation with human judgment

We use automation and AI-assisted work to reduce repetition. We review the output, verify material findings, and keep decisions with accountable people.

Ownership after insight

We connect each agreed priority to an owner, a next action, and a review date. We measure progress against a documented baseline.

Clear scope and data boundaries

We define deliverables, fees, responsibilities, and approved data channels before work begins. We keep patient information out of public marketing and inquiry systems.

How we put our mission into practice

We prioritize clients over clicks, evidence over unsupported claims, and execution over activity. We use technology without outsourcing our judgment. We sell capability without manufacturing credibility.

We are a Wyoming-incorporated business focused on evidence-based healthcare revenue operations. DIRT is our embedded data-intelligence capability, not a separate company. Our commitments below describe how we intend to operate; they are not claims of independent certification.

Truthful claims and accountable execution

We work to make service claims, proposed outcomes, and operational reporting accurate and verifiable. Demonstrations and modeled examples are identified as illustrative; financial results are not guaranteed.

Privacy-first commercial inquiries

Our public forms are for business inquiries, not patient information. Please do not send medical records, claim extracts, member identifiers, payment credentials, or other sensitive clinical information through our website or marketing channels.

We aim to limit access to the information needed for a task, use approved systems for sensitive work, and review third-party tools before granting access. Client-specific safeguards and agreements must be established before restricted healthcare data is accepted.

Respectful workplace and business conduct

Our operating principles oppose unlawful harassment, discrimination, retaliation, bribery, misleading claims, and fraudulent healthcare billing. We seek respectful collaboration and appropriate procedures for raising concerns.

These are public operating commitments, not proof of HIPAA certification, SOC 2 attestation, ISO certification, or completion of any external audit. For business questions or corrections, email info@rootrcm.com. Do not include PHI.

Eligibility-to-cash workflow

Revenue integrity begins when a visit is scheduled and ends when the account reconciles. Our workflow maps each dependency across intake, eligibility, authorizations, coding, submission, remittance, and patient balances.

Verify coverage and pre-service requirements before care.
Track clean-claim acceptance, rejections, and payer acknowledgment.

Denial root-cause taxonomy

Denial management works when repeated errors are grouped by cause, not merely by insurer. A controlled taxonomy distinguishes eligibility gaps, authorization failures, coding edits, timely filing, medical necessity, enrollment, and underpayment exceptions.

Tag each denial with a specific, reviewable cause.
Assign correction to its originating workflow and owner.
Measure overturn rate, rework, and preventable recurrence.
Credentialing and payer enrollment velocity

Credentialing delays can block otherwise collectible services before billing begins. We track the handoffs among CAQH, payer enrollment, effective dates, rosters, and EDI/ERA setup without treating an application submission as an approved contract.

Record application and payer-response timestamps.
Monitor effective dates, missing documents, and roster changes.
Validate claim and remittance readiness before go-live.
A claim is not operationally complete when it is submitted. It is complete when its financial outcome is reconciled.

Healthcare Revenue Intelligence: An ASC Denials Guide
Healthcare Revenue Intelligence: An ASC Denials Guide

Use healthcare revenue intelligence to investigate ASC denials, measure payer exposure, and prioritize recovery and prevention.

What is healthcare revenue intelligence?

Healthcare revenue intelligence connects billing, remittance, authorization, contract, and workflow data to explain where revenue is delayed or lost and what to do next. For an ambulatory surgery center (ASC), the objective is a decision: which denial pattern deserves intervention, who owns it, and how will leadership verify the result?

Why an ASC needs more than a denial dashboard

A dashboard can show unpaid balances without explaining their causes. ASC revenue operations need to distinguish facility reimbursement from professional billing, separate submission failures from adjudicated denials, and connect each exception to the applicable payer, procedure, service date, and operational handoff. An authorization obtained for one billing entity or setting should not be assumed to cover another.

Start with a reconciled financial picture

Connect practice-management claims and service lines to clearinghouse acknowledgements, payer remittances, adjustments, and cash posting. Retain authorization evidence and the contract version relevant to the service date. Reconcile source totals before drawing conclusions; isolate unmatched records, duplicate exports, reversals, and recoupments so that reporting does not turn accounting noise into apparent revenue opportunity.

Denial versus rejection versus underpayment

A rejection generally means a claim failed an acceptance edit; an adjudicated denial reflects a payer payment decision. An underpayment requires comparison with the applicable expected allowed amount and payment rules. Give each category its own queue and denominator rather than combining all three into one denial rate. A contractual adjustment is not automatically recoverable revenue.

Investigate authorization and eligibility mismatches

Compare the authorized procedure, units, dates, facility, provider, and setting with what was scheduled, performed, and billed. Route procedure changes back to the authorization owner before claim submission. Preserve dated payer responses and reference numbers; an authorization or an eligibility response alone does not establish that every condition of payment has been met.

The 2026 Medicare ASC authorization distinction

CMS operates a demonstration for selected ASC services in ten states. Its updated rollout permits requests from January 5, 2026 for services from January 19 in California, Florida, Tennessee, Pennsylvania, Maryland, Georgia, and New York; Texas, Arizona, and Ohio use February 2 and February 16 respectively. Targeted categories include blepharoplasty, botulinum toxin injections, panniculectomy, rhinoplasty, and vein ablation. [1]

Do not copy hospital outpatient rules into an ASC workflow

The ASC demonstration and the hospital outpatient prior authorization program are separate. Noridian explains that prior authorization is optional under the ASC demonstration, but bypassing it subjects applicable claims to prepayment review; its guidance also identifies Medicare Advantage among excluded claim types. Confirm the current CMS code list and the responsible Medicare Administrative Contractor instructions for the facility. [2]

Review coding, coverage, and payment configuration

Investigate recurring procedure and modifier combinations, documentation gaps, medical-necessity decisions, and site-of-service mismatches with qualified coding staff. Check the service-date version of Medicare ASC payment files and relevant coverage policies rather than assuming a procedure receives the same facility payment in every setting. CMS publishes ASC approved HCPCS codes and payment rates. [3]

Turn payer exposure into a decision queue

Group unresolved balances by payer, product, denial family, service period, and responsible workflow. Rank work using supported expected reimbursement, deadline proximity, documentation readiness, and recovery effort. Keep gross charges, expected allowed amounts, outstanding balances, and estimated recoverable amounts separate. A large billed balance can overstate the opportunity when contractual terms are ignored.

Measure denial incidence consistently

For an initial line-level denial rate, divide uniquely denied service lines at first adjudication by all service lines first adjudicated in the same cohort. Define how partial denials, zero-pay lines, secondary claims, and reversals are handled. Report a dollar-based measure separately, using a documented dollar basis; do not mix line counts, claim counts, and charge dollars. These are proposed operating definitions, not universal benchmarks.

Measure recovery and prevention separately

Track cash recovered for a defined denied cohort against that cohort’s documented collectible amount, alongside resolution time and unresolved value. Keep pending appeals out of realized recovery. For prevention, compare new denial incidence after a workflow change using comparable payer and procedure cohorts and enough adjudication runout. A cleared backlog does not prove that the upstream failure has stopped.

Control appeal deadlines by payer and appeal level

Assign an owner, deadline, evidence checklist, next action, and escalation date to each recoverable segment. CMS generally allows 120 days from receipt of the initial determination to request an Original Medicare redetermination. That is not a universal deadline for commercial plans, Medicaid, Medicare Advantage, or subsequent appeal levels; verify the governing rules and contract. [4]

A practical first-month operating plan

First, reconcile data and agree on definitions. Next, identify a narrow payer-and-denial segment with actionable evidence and name its owner. Then work the recoverable queue while correcting the originating authorization, coding, enrollment, or submission handoff. Finally, review cash results, unresolved exceptions, and new denial incidence; retain a weekly decision log so the team can distinguish completed activity from measurable improvement.

Where ROOT and DIRT fit

We approach revenue operations through Connect → Reconcile → Explain → Prioritize → Act → Measure. DIRT—Data Intelligence for Revenue Transformation—is our embedded intelligence capability. A practice-specific diagnostic should establish available data, reconciliation gaps, priority exposure, and feasible actions before committing to automation; this guide does not assert undocumented integrations or automated appeal capabilities.

Frequently asked: Is revenue intelligence the same as billing software?

Billing software supports transactions. Revenue intelligence adds a structured method for reconciling evidence, diagnosing variation, and assigning action across systems and teams. Its usefulness depends on source quality, consistent definitions, and follow-through rather than the number of charts.

Frequently asked: Can automation eliminate ASC denials?

No. Rules, contracts, documentation, clinical decisions, and payer adjudication can all affect payment. Automation can support exception routing and consistent checks, but disputed coding and coverage decisions need appropriate review. Start with a validated recurring workflow and measure both error rates and staff rework before expanding it.

Frequently asked: What data should leadership request?

Begin with aggregated payer-level denial counts and values, adjudication cohorts, aging, recovery status, and authorization exceptions. Use authorized access and the minimum necessary information for operational investigation. Do not send patient records, claim identifiers, or other protected health information through ROOT’s public inquiry form.
